steps.title: Beaujolais
steps.body: Beaujolais, just south of Burgundy, grows almost all of the world's Gamay. In the south, on clay and limestone, it makes simple Beaujolais. In the north, on pink granite and schist, it makes Beaujolais-Villages and the ten crus. Granite drains well and is poor, giving Gamay its best structure and perfume.

steps.title: Elsewhere
steps.body: Gamay grows in the Loire, in Touraine and Anjou, often for light reds and rosés, and in the Côte Roannaise. Switzerland blends it with Pinot Noir to make Dôle. It's appearing in Oregon, Canada's Niagara and Australia. Burgundy's Coteaux Bourguignons can include it.

steps.prompt: Match each place to its Gamay.

steps.body: Look for cru Beaujolais rather than plain Beaujolais. The ten crus, on granite, show what Gamay can really do, often at modest prices.

steps.explanation: Granite is poor, not fertile, and that helps.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Beaujolais grows almost all the world's Gamay
Northern granite gives the best wines
The Loire, Switzerland and Oregon grow some too
